column1: 35th_Birthday,"Celebrating 35 Years of Business","This year marks the 35th anniversary of Dorotape! ","<div id=""kskin_casestudies"" class=""kpadded"">

35 years is a long time in any business and we are genuinely grateful to not only still be working within the industry but also progressing and thriving in the marketplace too. We’ve been getting a little nostalgic, looking back at the old photo album reminiscing on how it all began. Read on for a potted history of Dorotape.

Our story begins in 1988. As part of a German / European group of companies, we became one of the first manufacturers of film application tape to supply the UK graphics market. The range quickly grew to include self-adhesive films. Something new to the market.
Mick Ingram joined the company in 1995 and was promoted to director in 2004. He steered the good ship Dorotape to independence in 2009 when we left our German sister company to go it alone.

As the business grew so too did the need for larger premises, three moves within Market harborough followed until in 2013 the business upped sticks to move to the other side of town of where we are still based today.

In 2021 Mick became the sole owner of Dorotape. Today we’re partners with over 20 global manufacturers, supplying specialist films and vinyl to all manner of industries. And we’re still growing and developing into new sectors, creating bespoke products for specialist projects and reaching people right across the world. There is never a dull moment.
This seems like the perfect time to say a huge thank you to all our loyal customers and suppliers for supporting us throughout the years. Here’s to the next 35!

There’s not a day that goes by here at Dorotape that we don’t field questions about application tape. With a wide range of tack levels and types of face film, choosing the right one is not always straightforward. To make life easier we’re here to untangle this sticky dilemma.

What is now Dorotape began life almost 35 years ago. As part of a European group of companies, we were one of the first to supply application tape to the UK signs and graphics market, so we’re confident that we can reliably be on hand to advise on which one is right for each job.

column2: >In brief, here’s a quick guide to which tape to use and when<span style=""color:#d7328a
Paper tapes are more suitable for wet application vinyl.
Clear filmic application tapes are the preferred choice if overlaying and aligning vinyl and films.
The most common tack level is medium to high tack which is suitable for most small to mid-sized graphics.
Low tack application tape is best for large sized vinyl graphics and lettering, wall graphics, frosted window films and stencil films.
Low-tack paper application tape is also ideal for protecting printed graphics during handling, storage and transport.
High-tack application tapes lend themselves to smaller sized graphics and lettering as well as high-tack self-adhesive films such as reflective vinyl.
Conform® paper application tapes feature 'Release Liner Adhesion' for an even adhesion to the backing liner without dog-earing.

column1: Most glitter films come with just a backing liner. Anyone familiar with the application of glitter vinyl will know that this can make them extremely tricky to apply, as using a squeegee to create a smooth and even application can create a horrible glittery mess. This also means the film is ideal for cad cutting, by cutting and weeding in reverse through the backing liner.

To apply SparkleColour simply remove the backing liner and apply it to the surface using a squeegee. When the vinyl is in position remove the protective top liner. And the result? A show-stopping vinyl that catches the light and the eye of any passerby.

Cast-Calendered,"Cast or calendered? Know your vinyl","Do you you know the key differences, benefits and limitations between the different types of self-adhesive vinyl (PVC)?","<div id=""kskin_casestudies"" class=""kpadded"">
It’s important to understand the key differences between the two but how well do you know your vinyl?

column2: >If you’re puzzled about which one to use here’s our quick guide to the benefits and limitations of the types and grades of vinyl<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: Firstly, for the record, all pvc vinyl is made one of two ways: cast or calendered. And we have both types.

Calendered vinyl is the most commonly used type by signmakers and large format printers. They start life as a solid resin that is melted together with a plasticiser to make it soft and flexible as well as a pigment to add colour. This is then compounded and as it cools, it is extruded, being drawn through a series of temperature controlled rollers which stretches and flattens the film to a uniform thickness
column4: . This is then wound into jumbo rolls ready to be coated with an adhesive and a liner added. Calendered films come in two main categories

column1: • Monomeric grade PVC is the most economical and least durable, best suited to interior and short-term exterior applications (5 years for black & white, 4 years for colours in the case of the Event Range) on to flat 1D and slightly curved 2D surfaces. The monomeric plasticisers used in their production to make the film softer and more flexible have a low molecular weight which after time, slowly migrates to the surface of the film causing it to shrink and become brittle. These films are therefore not suitable for demanding exterior applications such as vehicle graphics or fascia signage as it will almost certainly start to shrink back from the edges to reveal the adhesive beneath. Once this starts, any dirt in the atmosphere will quickly create a dirty grey outline around the graphics and eventually, the vinyl will begin to flake off like peeling paint.

• Polymeric grade vinyl uses polymeric plasticisers that have a more complex molecular chain meaning that this binds well together and they shrink back at a slower rate. This makes them more durable and with better UV and temperature resistance, suitable for longer term use outdoors on 1D and 2D surfaces (10 years for black & white, 8 years for colours in the case of the Platinum Range). If used on more complex curves, it is still recommended to cut and overlap seams as opposed to heating and stretching like you can a cast film.

Cast films are made differently to calendered films, starting off as a liquid which is then poured onto a casting sheet before moving slowly through a set of temperature-controlled ovens where the liquid evaporates leaving behind an extremely thin layer. This then gets rolled
column2: typically to 50µ or even as thin as 30µ. Cast films have little internal tension and are dimensionally stable, so shrinkage is barely perceptible. Cast films are thinner and softer, they are highly flexible and easier to apply over 3D curved surfaces using heat. With a durability in excess of 12 years (in the case of Ri-Jet C50 Ultimate, cast vinyl offers the ultimate in terms of durability.

Glass-Etch-Vinyl,"Glass Etch Vinyl - Wet or Dry Application?","To wet apply or dry apply? That is the question!","<div id=""kskin_casestudies"" class=""kpadded"">

When it comes to etched glass-effect vinyl and films the question we get asked the most by customers is whether we recommend a dry or wet apply product, we supply both kinds, by the way! The answer to this really does come down to the location of the glass, the environment, the complexity of the job and also the user’s preference.
Historically wet apply has been the go-to for applications, but with the introduction of impressive dry apply products to the market the usage of both is levelling up.

column2: >If you’re puzzled about which one to use here’s our quick guide to the benefits and limitations of both applications<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: This method is commonly used when applying large areas of etch glass vinyl but for this purpose we will assume here that we are applying some simple text or graphics using Float-On application fluid. It is also possible to substitute application fluid for some water with a couple of drops of Johnsons Baby Bath mixed by hand to produce a foamy solution.
Note: Graphics applied in low temperatures may suffer from reduced initial adhesion which can lead to problems later so it is best to apply at a minimum of 15oC.

Ensure that the glass has been cleaned adequately. First using warm soapy water, then with a degreaser such as isopropanol (or methylated spirit) and a lint free cloth or lint free wipes. Hardened debris such as paint spots can be removed with a blade flat against the glass. Particular attention should be payed to the edges of the glass panel and rubber seals to avoid dirt being drawn under the film.

Once the design has been cad-cut and weeded, cover the graphic with an application tape that has a good quality paper such as 900E or Conform ®: 4075RLA. and prepare the surface ready for the graphics.

To apply the graphics, simply spray the glass with a fine mist of your chosed application fluid, remove the backing liner from the etch glass vinyl, lightly spray the adhesive side and lay the graphics down onto the wet surface. As this layer of liquid acts as a barrier between the graphics and the substrate it reduces the adhesion level and makes it possible to make slight adjustments to the graphics position.

Once in the correct position dab down and apply pressure using a good quality squeegee and by working from the centre outwards remove all the liquid from underneath the graphics using a firm squeegee to enable the adhesive to key on to the glass.

When applying graphics wet, the adhesive takes longer to reach it's final adhesive strength so the more liquid is used the longer it takes before the graphics are firmly adhered. We recommend at least 1 hour before the next step.

Re-squeegee the entire area to make sure that the liquid has been completely expelled and carefully peel back the application tape diagonally at 180o to the surface and not lifting at 90o towards yourself as this can encourage air bubbles to form. Finally re-squeegee the entire graphics again paying particular attention to the edges and trimming 1mm-2mm from any rubber seals.

column2: Suitable for indoor and outdoor use
Ideal for areas which can experience moisture such as hair salons and launderettes

column1: Using our Dry Apply Etch Glass films is easy whether you are cutting logos and lettering or applying one large piece to the glass. These etched glass vinyls must be applied 'dry' using a soft squeegee such as a felt edged squeegee
Glass surface preparation is just as important here as it was with the wet apply method so take time to thoroughly clean.
If cutting out a design with pre-spaced elements you will first need to cad-cut and weed the waste away, then cover the graphic with an application tape such as Conform ®
column2: 4761RLA which is specifically designed for use with dry apply films.

column1: Once you are ready to apply, establish exactly where the graphics need to be positioned and fix in place by using small tabs of 50mm wide masking tape. Then use a strip of 50mm masking tape the full width of the graphic and create a hinge by fixing this along the top of the graphic, half on the application tape of the graphic and half on the glass.

To apply the glass etch vinyl, lift the graphic up from the glass, folding it back on the hinge, then loosen and peel down about 150mm of the backing liner before lowering the now exposed film back down into place on to the glass, while at the same time applying squeegee pressure starting at the centre and working down and towards each edge in turn in overlapping strokes. Remove another 150mm or so of backing liner and repeat the process until the graphic is applied.

It is also possible to use this hinge method for larger lettering applications by slitting up between each letter, pairs of letters or groups of letters once the top hinge has been applied and applying these separately. Similarly, for long narrow graphics it is possible to fix the hinge on the left or right hand side instead of the top.
Now remove the application tape by carefully peeling it back diagonally at 180° to the surface and not lifting at 90° towards yourself as this can encourage air bubbles to form.
Finally re-squeegee the entire graphics again paying particular attention to the edges and trimming 1mm-2mm from any rubber seals using a sharp knife.
You will see from this video just how easy it is to apply and how any remaining creases or bubbles can be removed using heat and a squeegee.

column2: >Choosing the right product for advertising on retail windows—where clean and easy removability is essential—can be confusing. Finding a solution that saves both time and money is key<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: Traditionally, the go-to material for temporary window graphics would have been Static Cling Vinyl. This PVC-based film relies on the static electrical charge within the film to attract (cling) to a surface that has an opposite charge such as glass without the need of adhesive.
While Static Cling Vinyl offers some benefits, it has significant downsides:
• Environmental concerns – Being a highly plasticised PVC film, it is one of the worst plastics for the environment.
• Limited shelf life – The material degrades after about six months as plasticisers migrate out of the PVC, leading to a less flexible film and a reduction in its effectiveness.
• Performance issues – It struggles in colder conditions and high-humidity environments such as beauty salons and launderettes.

Glass Apeel window graphic material works differently, utilising something called van der Waals force. Its smooth, non-sticky underside has a microporous layer that expands the film's surface area, creating a dull, grip-like feel. When applied to a smooth surface such as glass or metal, the film naturally aligns with it, keeping it firmly in place.
To remove it, simply peel from one corner—the alignment breaks, and the grip releases instantly, leaving no residue.

Glass Apeel is available in transparent clear and white with block-out properties. It is printable using Latex, UV, and Eco-solvent inks, making it easy to create effective advertising on glass, acrylic, and other smooth surfaces.
• Easy to install – Completely repositionable and fully reusable
• Eco-friendly – Free from PVC, Phthalates and VOCs
• Temperature-resistant – Stays flat and performs well in varying conditions without shrinkage
• Use dry or wet application on clean and degreased smooth substrates at temperatures above 10oC
• Printed media should dry for at least 24 hours before lamination
• Transparent – is 100% optically clear for use on glass and acrylic and can be front or mirror printed
• White – 99% light block-out for windows and smooth metal surfaces
• Frosted – has a bright translucency for front or mirror printing, providing privacy while letting light through
• Solar – is a transparent film with energy conservation properties for use on windows to help maintain an even indoor temperature

Heat-Transfer-Vinyl,"Heat Transfer Vinyl Do's and Don'ts","Find out all you need to know about selecting the right HTV for the job!","<div id=""kskin_casestudies"" class=""kpadded"">

Using heat transfer vinyl (HTV) is a fantastic way of adding branding, lettering, numbering and imagery to sportswear, workwear, bags and other materials. But to get long-lasting results there are some definite do’s and don’ts. Here is our quick guide:

column2:
Find out what the material you are applying to is made from.
Sounds obvious but you'd be surprised how many times this causes confusion. The reason this is super important is because an htv film designed to transfer on to cotton will have different properties than one that is designed to be applied to polyester fabric.

Consider whether you need block out or not.
When transferring onto polyester fabric it is important that the htv has an added layer to offer dye-blocking capabilities. This will stop any dye migration from the garment showing through the vinyl

Think about whether you need to reverse your design
This is crucial for success and is probably the most forgotton rule on the HTV world. Coloured HTV requires reverse cutting as you are going to wedd it then flip it over and press it on to he garment using the clear liner as it's own application tape. However, if you are digitally printing the design you treat this like a regular print and cut film, before using a special heat proof application tape such as Transprint to transfer it to the garment for pressing.

Check the recommended time and temp settings for the HTV you are using.
Again, this is critical but sometimes easy to be complacent so make sure you double check the specific pressure and time advised for transferring on to the garments. We have everything available for you on our website so there should't be any confusion.

Don’t forget to consider the wash resistance needed.
Nobody wants to receive garments back from their clients with the lettering hanging off so it is important to know what the limitations are when it comes to laundering. We have everything you need to know so if you can't see it on the website please just give us a call and ask one of the team.

Don’t forget to have a can of Flex Off ready for any mishaps.
Accidents can happen and customers can change their minds so it’s best to be prepared just in case.

Don’t forget to contact us if you’re not sure which HTV to use and need some advice.
We’re always happy to help!

HTV-Reflective,"Shining a light on reflective HTV","It’s that time of year when the nights start drawing in. If you are working outside or taking part in any outdoor leisure or sporting activities, you need to consider the safety benefits of being seen in the dark.","<div id=""kskin_casestudies"" class=""kpadded"">

When it comes to reflective heat transfer vinyl (HTV), you’d think the options would be pretty straightforward, but in fact, there are many different variants. To confuse matters more, we have recently expanded our range to provide an even wider choice in terms of quality as well as budget.

column2: >Reflective HTV: what is it and how does it work<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: All reflective HTV is made up of metallised microscopic glass beads which reflect light directly back towards its source, therefore making the material appear bright and highly visible in darkened conditions. This retroreflective glass bead surface is overlaminated with a transparent PET film to aid cad-cutting. It’s also coated with a dry heat-activated adhesive backing for heat pressing onto a wide range of fabrics.

column2: >What can reflective HTV be used on<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: Reflective HTV is suitable for transferring onto textiles such as cotton, uncoated nylon, mixtures of polyester/cotton and polyester/acrylic. Depending on which film is selected, the cad-cut lettering, logos and safety markings can be heat pressed onto workwear, safety clothing, sportswear, leisurewear and promotional items.

column2: First up is the ever-popular Silva-Lite material, which is a high-quality UK-produced material designed for the cad-cutting of garment lettering and logos. The minimum retroreflective value conforms to EN ISO 20471:2013 making it perfect for a wide variety of uses.

Our Reflex Black reflective HTV offers something completely different. The black surface of the film looks standard in the daytime but when hit by direct light in darkened conditions the reflective colour turns bright silver white. Ideal for adding inconspicuous branding to any item.

Also in our range is the Poli-Flex 4783 silver reflective HTV that has a ‘turbo’ adhesive. The main benefit of using this material is that it can be applied at a lower temperature and for a shorter time, giving time and cost savings. It’s also suitable for a wider range of materials and items. Conforms to EN ISO 20471:2013

Finally, and at the top end of the reflective HTV range is the Poli-Flex 4781 which uses 3M® Scotchlite film. This film offers the highest level of visibility as well as guaranteeing a secure and long-lasting bond to the textile. Ideal for hi-vis safety wear and a must for anyone working on our roads. Conforms to EN ISO 20471:2013

column1: Don’t be mistaken in thinking these films are only necessary after the clocks have changed. They also provide safety in low-light conditions, such as rain and snow. As well as the safety aspect of these films, they can also add something unusual to leisurewear and clothing such as dancewear too, great for subtle branding.

MagvFerro,"Magnetic vinyl vs. ferrous film: What’s the difference and which should you choose?","Magnetic vinyl vs. ferrous film: What’s the difference and which should you choose? - Explaining the differences in films.","<div id=""kskin_casestudies"" class=""kpadded"">

If you’re working with graphics, signage, or display systems, you’ve probably come across magnetic vinyl and ferrous film. While they’re often used together, these materials have very different properties and understanding how each one works, and how to pair them correctly, can help you save time, reduce waste, and improve the look and flexibility of your display setup.
In this post, we break down what each material is, how they work and the best ways to use them for your next project.

Ferrous Film is a flexible material that contains iron powder, making it magnetically receptive. In other words, magnetic materials and objects will easily attract to its surface. This makes it ideal for applications where you want to layer or change graphics quickly and efficiently.

Ferrous film is available in both self-adhesive and non-adhesive forms. The non-adhesive version is often used as an interchangeable face layer over a magnetic base, while the self-adhesive version is commonly used to create a magnetically receptive surface on walls, doors, or other smooth surfaces. Some ferrous films have a plain grey-brown finish for use with magnetic overlays, while others are printable, allowing for custom graphics. You’ll also find writable options with whiteboard or chalkboard finishes - perfect for classrooms, offices or reusable signage.

Lightweight and easy to handle, ferrous film is also an eco-friendly option, with PVC-free varieties available. It can be rolled, cut and transported easily, making it well-suited for projects across the UK and beyond.
• Lightweight and flexible for easy transport and installation
• PVC-free and reusable options for eco-conscious users

Magnetic Vinyl is the counterpart to ferrous film. Instead of being purely magnet receptive, it contains magnetised material and is designed to attach directly to steel or other ferrous surfaces (metals containing iron). It is available in different thicknesses and magnetic strengths, and is a popular choice for signage, retail displays and even vehicle graphics. It is important to remember that magnetic vinyl will not attract to vehicles that incorporate aluminium in their construction.

Thicker magnetic vinyl offers a stronger hold and is ideal for demanding situations, such as vehicle graphics, where staying in place at high speeds is essential. Thinner versions are more suited to light-duty uses like POS displays, posters, or signage.

Magnetic vinyl is available in both self-adhesive and non-adhesive forms. The non-adhesive type is popular for temporary displays that need to be applied and removed easily. The self-adhesive version can be applied to non-metal surfaces to create a magnetic base, allowing you to attach ferrous film on top for a versatile, changeable system.
It is worth noting that if you try and apply a magnetic vinyl on to another magnetic vinyl you will always have trouble lining the two layers up edge to edge due to the polarity.
• Quick to apply and remove to steel and ferrous surfaces - great for temporary or seasonal signage
• Printable options available for direct graphic application
• Suitable for indoor or outdoor use, including vehicles and retail spaces

column2: >How to choose the right combination<span style=""color:#009ee3

column1: When deciding between self-adhesive and non-adhesive options, consider how the display will be used and how often it needs to be updated.

For spaces that need regular updates, like event venues or retail displays, a self-adhesive base combined with a non-adhesive face is ideal. This setup lets you swap out graphics quickly without damaging walls or surfaces.
• Example: ASLAN FF410 (ferrous) + 9052 or 9056 (magnetic)
If you're designing a removable vehicle sign, non-adhesive magnetic vinyl is your best option. It’s easy to take on and off, and its strength ensures the graphic stays put while driving.
If you're looking to create a writable blackboard surface that also holds magnetic tools or displays, opt for a self-adhesive ferrous film with a blackboard face and magnetic receptiveness.
Use: Self-adhesive ferrous film with blackboard finish
And if you're looking for a dry wipe surface that also supports magnetic tools or displays, go with a self-adhesive ferrous film featuring a whiteboard surface and magnetic receptivity.
Use: Self-adhesive ferrous film with whiteboard finish

column2: >Need help with your next project<span style=""color:#009ee3

column1: When used correctly, magnetic vinyl and ferrous film offer a highly flexible, reusable and professional solution for everything from signage to interactive displays. Whether you're building a dynamic retail setup or updating vehicle graphics, choosing the right material, or combination, makes the entire process smoother and more efficient.

Mono_vs_Poly,"Monomeric vs polymeric calendered vinyl: shrinkage, durability & uses","Learn the difference between monomeric and polymeric calendered vinyl, including plasticisers, shrinkage, durability, and how each performs in graphic applications.","<div id=""kskin_casestudies"" class=""kpadded"">
It’s important to understand the key differences between the two but how well do you know your vinyl?

column2: >Monomeric vs polymeric calendered vinyl: shrinkage, durability & uses<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: Learn the difference between monomeric and polymeric calendered vinyl, including plasticisers, shrinkage, durability, and how each performs in graphic applications.

column2: >Monomeric vs polymeric calendared vinyl: understanding shrinkage and performance<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: Calendared vinyl is one of the most commonly used materials in the sign and graphics industry. Its popularity comes from its versatility, wide availability, and cost efficiency. However, not all calendared vinyl performs the same. Understanding the difference between monomeric and polymeric calendared vinyl and how shrinkage affects performance is essential to achieving predictable, long lasting results.

Calendared vinyl starts as a solid PVC resin. During manufacturing, the resin is heated and combined with a plasticiser, which gives the material flexibility, along with pigments that add colour. The softened compound is then drawn through a series of heated, temperature controlled rollers that stretch and flatten it into a uniform film, typically between 70 and 100 microns thick.

Once formed, the vinyl is wound into large rolls, coated with a pressure sensitive adhesive, and finished with a release liner. This process makes calendared vinyl economical to produce and suitable for a wide range of graphic applications. Calendared films are generally divided into two categories: monomeric and polymeric.

column2: >The role of plasticisers in vinyl graphics<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: The key difference between monomeric and polymeric vinyl lies in the type of plasticiser used.

In graphics applications, the most common plasticiser families are phthalates, typically associated with monomeric vinyl, and adipates, most often associated with polymeric vinyl. These plasticisers differ in molecular structure, which directly affects flexibility, stability, and long term behaviour.

Phthalate based plasticisers have shorter molecular chains, meaning that they easily migrate to the surface of the vinyl and to the adhesive, while adipate based plasticisers use longer, more complex chains that are also more stable and take longer to migrate. This difference is central to how each vinyl type shrinks and ages over time.

Monomeric calendared vinyl is the most economical option and is widely used for interior graphics and short term exterior applications. It is best suited to flat (1D) and slightly curved (2D) surfaces, where minimal stress is placed on the film.

Because monomeric vinyl relies on low molecular weight plasticisers, these plasticisers gradually migrate to the surface as the material ages. This migration causes the vinyl to shrink and slowly lose flexibility, eventually becoming brittle.

Typical durability is around five years for black and white films and four years for coloured films, depending on exposure and conditions. For temporary signage, promotional graphics, and short life displays, this level of performance is often sufficient. However, in more demanding outdoor applications, shrinkage can become noticeable as the vinyl pulls back from edges and corners.
View all of our Monomeric Vinyl here.

Polymeric calendared vinyl is designed for greater dimensional stability and longer term use. It uses polymeric plasticisers, commonly adipates, which bind more effectively within the PVC structure and migrate far more slowly.

As a result, polymeric vinyl exhibits reduced shrinkage, improved resistance to UV exposure, and better performance across temperature changes. This makes it suitable for long term outdoor graphics on flat and gently curved surfaces.

Polymeric films typically offer durability of around ten years for black and white films and eight years for coloured films, depending on the product range. While they can handle gentle curves, they are not intended for deep recesses or complex three dimensional shapes.
View all of our Polymeric Vinyl here.

column2: >How shrinkage affects installation and appearance<span style=""color:#d7328a

column1: Shrinkage is a natural characteristic of calendared vinyl, but its impact varies significantly between monomeric and polymeric grades. As vinyl shrinks, it attempts to return to its original, unstressed state. This movement can lead to edge pull back, corner lifting, and gaps between panels in multi panel graphics.

On curved surfaces, shrinkage can introduce tension that increases the likelihood of lifting over time. In printed graphics, uneven shrinkage may also cause subtle distortion, particularly noticeable in logos or precise text alignment. Temperature changes can accelerate these effects, especially in exterior environments.

Ultimately, the choice between monomeric and polymeric calendared vinyl is a balance between cost, expected lifespan, and dimensional stability. Monomeric vinyl provides a cost effective solution for short term, low stress applications, while polymeric vinyl offers improved stability and appearance retention for longer term use.
Understanding how plasticiser chemistry influences shrinkage helps ensure more reliable performance and better long term visual results.

Sandblasting-Shotpeening,"Sandblasting and Shotpeening","An in-depth look into sandblasting and shot peening","<div id=""kskin_casestudies"" class=""kpadded"">

Not only do we supply specialist self-adhesive films to the retail design, display and graphics sectors, but we also play a major part in supplying industrial-grade stencil films to various industries both in the UK and abroad. Consider it our best-kept secret!

Offering protection to a wide variety of substrates including wood, slate, glass, stone and metal, our tough stencil films are used to mask off areas during the processes of sandblasting and shot peening.

Used to decorate and personalise signs and plaques made from wood, glass and slate, the sandblasting process requires strong stencil film. ASLAN supplies stencil films ranging from 80 micron to 250 micron thick which are perfect for these light-to-medium-duty sandblasting projects.

Higher-pressure sandblasting requires a more robust stencil film. This is typically used by stone masons when crafting headstones and other memorials, as well as decorative features in the construction industry and ornamental areas in public spaces. Products that are commonly used to mask off and protect areas during these heavy-duty sandblasting jobs range from 330 micron to 600 micron.

The shot peening of metal surfaces and components involves firing small ‘shot’ at high speed into a metal surface. This increases the density and strengthens that area, which in turn makes it highly resistant to fatigue and failure.

Due to the critical nature of some of these components, it’s super important to use the right stencil film. We’ve been working alongside a number of customers involved in the Automotive, Aviation and Aerospace industries, as well as those manufacturing pipes, valves and pumps for the Water, Oil and Gas sectors, to develop new products that offer increased adhesion values to cope with this rigorous process.
